analysis.one_liner: Taxes fossil fuels by carbon content, returns most revenue to households as annual dividends.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in October 2011 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge an excise tax on coal, oil, and natural gas based on how much carbon dioxide they produce when burned, starting at $10 per ton and rising $10 each year until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of 1990 levels. Most of the money would be paid out equally to every lawful resident as an annual 'consumer dividend,' protecting households from higher energy prices; the rest could reduce deficits. Energy-intensive industries would pay far more, while the tax revenue recycled to consumers would be a net gain for most lower- and middle-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households come out ahead under the design: the annual dividend is paid per person, so lower- and middle-income families — who use less energy than the wealthy — would typically receive more back than they pay in higher fuel prices. Renewable energy and low-carbon industries gain a growing price advantage over fossil fuels. The bill's findings also project deficit reduction of more than $480 billion over ten years from the first years of revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and other energy fuels equal to $10 per ton of carbon dioxide from combustion, rising $10 per year until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of 1990 levels.
Returns revenue to individuals through an annual consumer dividend to every eligible lawful resident, explicitly to protect consumers from higher energy prices.
Appropriates the tax collected at the initial $10 rate to the Healthy Climate Trust Fund for dividend payments, with amounts above $10 per ton available for other purposes such as deficit reduction.
The bill's stated findings project that a $10-per-ton carbon tax could reduce the deficit by more than $480 billion over ten years.
Includes border adjustments so imported products from countries without a comparable carbon tax pay an equalizing fee, protecting U.S. manufacturers from undercutting.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and importers — coal companies, oil and gas producers, and natural gas suppliers — would pay the tax directly and pass much of it to consumers through higher prices for electricity, gasoline, and heating. Energy-intensive industries like manufacturing, airlines, and utilities would face sharply rising fuel costs as the rate climbs $10 per ton every year. Higher-income households, which consume the most energy, would pay more in higher prices than they receive in dividends.

drawbacks.text: The tax starts at $10 per ton and rises $10 each year without a cap, so energy prices would climb steadily — critics argued this would raise costs for households and hurt energy-intensive industries even with the dividend offsetting much of it.
If emissions do not fall fast enough, the tax keeps rising automatically, which supporters saw as certainty but which gives industry and consumers little relief if clean alternatives develop slowly.

Recycling revenue through an annual dividend reduces the deficit-reduction potential: only revenue above the initial $10-per-ton rate goes to deficit reduction, and dividend payments would add to taxable income but still count as federal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is deliberately progressive: because the dividend is paid per person while wealthier households buy more energy, most working families would come out ahead financially, and the bill included border adjustments to shield U.S. manufacturers. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive industries, and energy prices would rise even where households are made whole on average — a family with a long commute or oil heating could pay more than it gets back. The automatic annual escalator with no revenue cap is the strongest good-faith objection: it prioritizes emissions targets over price certainty.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in October 2011 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the Save Our Climate Act of 2011 on October 24, 2011, with eight original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced.
22 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further legislative action was recorded after the referral for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas companies were better off because the bill died without a vote — they avoided a carbon tax that would have climbed $10 per ton annually. Ordinary households lost the chance at an annual dividend payment designed to leave most of them financially ahead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, spared the tax

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled during the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote; with a Republican chair controlling the committee calendar, no floor action was possible.

industries.note: Coal has the highest carbon content per unit of energy of any fuel in the bill, so it would bear the largest tax per dollar of energy sold and would face the steepest competitive loss to natural gas and renewables.

Petroleum products and natural gas are taxable fuels, so producers and importers would pay the tax directly and pass it through in gasoline and heating prices; their interest in blocking the bill ran against consumers' interest in the dividend.
Utilities burning coal or gas would face escalating fuel costs each year, pushing them toward renewables or rate increases.
A rising carbon price would make wind, solar, and other low-carbon sources increasingly cost-competitive against fossil fuels without requiring a subsidy.
